addressed_problems.content: While iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) can identify sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) in vision-and-language (VL) models, the practical inference speedup of these subnetworks on hardware supporting unstructured pruning remains unmeasured. The paper only reports accuracy retention at various sparsity levels but does not evaluate end-to-end latency or throughput on runtimes such as XNNPACK. Without such hardware-aware evaluation, the real-world efficiency gains from the discovered lottery tickets for VL models are not demonstrated, leaving the practical deployment benefits of unstructured pruning in VL systems an open question.

The study of lottery tickets in region-feature-based VL models (UNITER, LXMERT) was limited to the multimodal fusion transformer, while the object detection module used for visual feature extraction was kept intact and not pruned. For end-to-end models, only ViLT was examined, and the exploration of other end-to-end VL architectures (e.g., PixelBERT, ALBEF) was not performed. Thus, whether matching subnetworks exist within the object detection component itself, and whether full end-to-end detection+fusion pipelines can be effectively pruned to yield winning tickets, remains unresolved. Addressing this gap would enable more comprehensive compression of practical VL systems that include both detection and fusion.

The original lottery ticket hypothesis posits that a matching subnetwork can achieve the exact accuracy of the full dense model when trained in isolation. In the context of vision-and-language pre-training, the paper finds that such strict matching is generally not achievable for most VL tasks; only 'relaxed' winning tickets (matching 99% of full accuracy) are observed at moderate sparsities (50%–70%). Whether strict matching can be attained under alternative training setups, rewinding strategies, or different architectures remains an open scientific question. Resolving this would clarify the validity of the lottery ticket hypothesis in multimodal settings and inform expectations for lossless compression.

Empirical results reveal significant task-specific and architecture-specific differences in pruneability: the VCR task requires lower sparsity (50%) to maintain performance compared to other tasks (up to 70% for VQA), and ViLT admits a much lower maximum sparsity (30%) than UNITER or LXMERT (70%). The paper offers hypotheses—such as that commonsense reasoning in VCR relies more on small weights, or that ViLT's single transformer must concentrate all modeling capacity—but the underlying mechanistic causes for these differences are not established. Understanding why certain tasks and architectures are harder to prune without performance loss is necessary for designing models that are inherently more compressible and for developing task-adaptive pruning strategies.

The iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) procedure used to identify winning tickets is computationally expensive, requiring multiple train-prune-retrain cycles, which is especially burdensome for large pre-trained vision-and-language models. The paper does not explore more efficient alternative methods such as one-shot pruning heuristics, early-bird ticket detection, or gradient-flow preserving initializations, which could potentially reduce the cost of ticket discovery. Developing such methods remains an unresolved challenge, and their effectiveness for VL models is unknown. Addressing this would make the practical application of lottery tickets to VLP more feasible and scalable.

Large-scale vision-and-language pre-trained (VLP) models (examples: UNITER, LXMERT, ViLT) provide strong, general multimodal representations but contain very large numbers of parameters, producing a high memory and computation footprint that impedes deployment in resource-constrained settings. Prior methods for making VLP models smaller focus on architectural design (compact backbones) or knowledge distillation, but it is unknown whether the parameter redundancy of pre-trained VLP models can be exploited by finding sparse, trainable subnetworks (i.e., lottery tickets) that preserve downstream-task performance and cross-task transferability. Related findings for the lottery ticket hypothesis exist in image classification and language modeling, but whether matching or "winning" subnetworks exist in pre-trained VLP models, whether such subnetworks transfer from pre-training to diverse downstream VL tasks, and how pruning interacts with different VLP architectures and training regimes (e.g., adversarial training) were unresolved. Additionally, finding subnetworks via iterative train-prune-retrain procedures is computationally expensive for large pre-trained VLP models, so it is unclear if task-agnostic (pre-training) pruning can amortize that cost while still yielding universally transferable subnetworks. These gaps prevent principled compression of VLP models: researchers and practitioners lack (i) knowledge of achievable sparsity levels that retain near-full accuracy across common VL tasks, (ii) understanding of whether masks learned on pre-training or on individual downstream tasks generalize across tasks, and (iii) clarity about how pruning interacts with VLP architectural choices (one-stream vs two-stream vs end-to-end) and with alternative training objectives (e.g., adversarial training).

nodes.content: In the context of pre-trained vision-and-language models used for downstream tasks such as VQA, VCR, NLVR², visual entailment, referring expression comprehension, and image-text retrieval, practitioners need compressed models that retain task performance: smaller models enable deployment on constrained hardware and reduce inference cost. Prior to this work, it was unknown whether sparse subnetworks that can be trained in isolation from the pre-trained VLP initialization exist for each downstream task (the standard LTH winning-ticket question) because existing LTH evidence focused on vision-only or language-only models or on smaller networks. Conventional approaches (naive unstructured random pruning, standard distillation, or ad-hoc compact architectures) either degrade performance or change the training pipeline; consequently, there was no quantification of achievable sparsity that still preserves near-full task accuracy for pre-trained VLP backbones, nor clarity about whether task-specific pruning could produce subnetworks that are trainable from the pre-trained initialization without extensive additional mechanisms (e.g., costly rewinding). This lack of knowledge prevented principled compression choices for VLP models and left open whether per-task IMP is a viable route to practical parameter reduction for common VL tasks.

The iterative draw-and-validate process for finding task-specific subnetworks (IMP per task) is computationally intensive when applied to large pre-trained VLP models, making it impractical to perform for each downstream task. If a single task-agnostic subnetwork could be identified from pre-training that transfers well to many downstream tasks, the cost of ticket discovery could be amortized. Before this work, it was unresolved whether IMP performed during VLP pre-training would learn a mask that: (a) preserves important cross-modal representations learned during pre-training, and (b) yields subnetworks that, after reinitialization to the pre-trained weights and downstream finetuning, achieve near-full accuracy across heterogeneous VL tasks. Without such a finding, practitioners lacked a practical route to obtain a single compressed VLP model usable across tasks without per-task expensive pruning.

For compression to be practically useful, it is important to know whether a subnetwork found for one downstream VL task overfits to that task's idiosyncrasies, or whether it encodes broadly useful multimodal structure that generalizes to other VL tasks. If task-specific masks do not transfer, per-task IMP is required, amplifying computational cost and limiting utility. Prior to this study, the transfer behavior among downstream VL tasks for IMP-derived masks was unquantified, so it was unclear whether masks learned for one task would be reusable for others (which would reduce the need for repeated pruning).

The original LTH evidence in vision and NLP suggests model architecture and input representations can influence the degree of redundant parameters removable by pruning. VLP literature contains different backbone designs: models that operate on object-region features (UNITER, LXMERT) and models that operate end-to-end on raw image patches (ViLT). It was unresolved whether LTH findings for region-feature-based VLP models generalize to patch-based end-to-end VLP models, and whether architectural choices constrain achievable sparsity while retaining downstream accuracy. Without this knowledge, recommendations for compressing VLP models could not be tailored to different backbone designs, and it remained unclear whether end-to-end VLP models are more or less amenable to unstructured pruning than region-feature-based models.

The original LTH formulation attributes winning-ticket behavior to the conjunction of a sparse mask and a favorable initialization. In VLP models, the role of the pre-trained multimodal weights versus general language pre-training (BERT) or random perturbations had not been empirically quantified. Specifically, it was unknown whether the mask alone is sufficient (i.e., any reasonable initialization would work) or whether the original pre-trained multimodal weights are necessary for the identified subnetwork to be trainable. Without this assessment, the relative importance of mask structure vs. weight values for achieving compressed yet high-performing VLP subnetworks was uncertain.

Prior LTH work showed that rewinding to weights from an early training iteration can be necessary to find winning tickets in large networks. It was therefore unclear whether rewinding is required when using pre-trained VLP initializations and finetuning for downstream VL tasks, or whether the original pre-trained initialization is already close enough to the desired basin. This question affects the practical workflow for ticket extraction: if rewinding is necessary, more complex checkpointing and extra computation are required; if not, the simpler reset-to-pretrained protocol suffices.

Robust or alternative training objectives such as adversarial training are used in VLP to improve generalization and robustness, but it was unknown whether LTH phenomena persist under such training or whether adversarial objectives fundamentally change the sparsity–performance tradeoff. Practically, if AT could enable sparser subnetworks with maintained accuracy, it would provide a pathway to further compression without sacrificing robustness or accuracy; conversely, if AT disrupted ticket existence, it would limit the applicability of LTH-based compression under robust training regimens.

Understanding why some source-task masks transfer better than others requires quantifying how similar sparsity patterns are across tasks. Prior to this analysis, it was unclear whether masks obtained under different supervision signals converge to similar sparse structures (which would explain universal transfer) or whether they diverge, implying task-specific pruning practices. Without this insight, explanations for observed transfer successes or failures remained speculative.

A "relaxed winning ticket" is defined as a subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$ obtained by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) whose re-trained performance on a downstream task reaches at least 99% of the full dense model accuracy for that task. For UNITER (a one-stream vision-and-language pre-trained model with pre-trained initialization $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$), task-specific IMP applied during finetuning yields relaxed winning tickets with highest sparsities ranging from 50% up to 70% depending on the task: e.g., Visual Question Answering (VQA) and several retrieval/recognition tasks admit such tickets at 70% sparsity while more demanding commonsense tasks (Visual Commonsense Reasoning, VCR) admitted up to 50% sparsity. The identified subnetworks are formed by a binary mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{T}}\in\{0,1\}^{d_1}$ for a downstream task $\mathcal{T}$ applied elementwise to the pre-trained weights, and when reinitialized to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ and re-trained on the same downstream task, they retain at least 99% of the full-model accuracy.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is supported by positive results across 7 diverse tasks (H1) and controlled baselines (H2) that demonstrate the non-triviality of the tickets. The main load-bearing uncertainties are measurement-related: the reliance on an unreported mini-dev set for VQA (P1) and the lack of variance estimates for some key results (P2). P1 directly threatens the quantitative claim for VQA, one of the flagship tasks; P2 threatens the robustness of the 99% threshold for several tasks where the margin is small. H1 and H2 provide strong generalization and comparative evidence but do not directly address P1 (the mini-dev set is a separate measurement validity issue) or P2 (single runs remain uncertain regardless of baselines). The conclusion is credible for the qualitative existence and approximate sparsity range, but the precise quantitative threshold (99%) and its reliability for VQA are less firmly established.

nodes.title: Task-specific relaxed winning tickets exist in UNITER at 50%–70% sparsity

nodes.content: Performing Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on the vision-and-language pre-training (VLP) objective (using the pre-training data and tasks of the UNITER vision-and-language pre-trained model) produces a task-agnostic mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{P}$ such that the subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{P}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$, when reinitialized to the original pre-trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ and fine-tuned on diverse downstream vision-and-language (VL) tasks, matches on average 98% of the full dense-model accuracy at 60% sparsity and 96% at 70% sparsity across the seven evaluated downstream tasks (average computed over Visual Question Answering (VQA), GQA, Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR), Natural Language Visual Reasoning for Real (NLVR²), Stanford Natural Language Inference - Visual Entailment (SNLI-VE), Referring Expression Comprehension on RefCOCO+, and Flickr30k retrieval metrics).

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 is backed by comprehensive multi-task evaluation (H3) showing consistent transfer at 60% and 70% sparsity. However, two load-bearing uncertainties are present: the reduced pre-training steps (P3) and the data overlap between pre-training and downstream tasks (P4). P3 threatens the optimality of the mask; P4 threatens the inference of universal knowledge transfer versus data-specific familiarity. H3 provides strong quantitative support but cannot resolve P4 because it relies on the same overlapping data. The interaction between P3 and P4 is partially offsetting: if the reduced steps yield a suboptimal mask, the true universal ticket might be even better, but P4 suggests the observed performance might be inflated. The conclusion is reliable for the particular population of tasks with overlapping image domains; its universality beyond that remains uncertain. The average performance drops are robust but the attribution of causality to pre-training knowledge is weakened by P4.

nodes.title: Task-agnostic (pre-training) IMP yields universally transferable subnetworks at 60%–70% sparsity

nodes.content: Subnetworks obtained by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on a specific downstream source task $\mathcal{S}$ (i.e., masks $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{S}}$) typically maintain strong performance when re-trained on other target tasks $\mathcal{T}$. Across the evaluated task pairs, task-specific tickets generally transfer reasonably, often retaining the majority of the source-task ticket's effectiveness on different target tasks, with substantial accuracy preserved across sparsities up to high pruning ratios.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 is strongly supported by the comprehensive pairwise transfer study (H4), which covers many source-target combinations and shows consistently positive transfer. The main weak point (P5) concerns the lack of error bars and quantitative thresholds for the transfer curves, making the claim "transfer reasonably well" somewhat vague. However, the visual consistency across many combinations suggests the qualitative direction is robust; the uncertainty is more about the precise magnitude of transfer. The conclusion is credible at the qualitative level, and H4 provides strong generalization evidence. The quantitative aspect (e.g., "majority of effectiveness retained") is less precisely supported, but overall the conclusion is well-grounded.

nodes.title: Task-specific subnetworks transfer well across downstream VL tasks

nodes.content: The lottery-ticket hypothesis (LTH) is observed across different vision-and-language pre-training (VLP) architectures: (a) For LXMERT (a two-stream architecture with object-region inputs), Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) can identify relaxed winning tickets (maintaining at least 99% of full-model accuracy) with achievable sparsity comparable to UNITER (up to approximately 70% in evaluated tasks) while preserving near-full accuracy. (b) For ViLT (an end-to-end, patch-based one-stream architecture that directly consumes image patches), IMP yields subnetworks that preserve performance only up to substantially lower sparsity (effective highest sparsity without impairing performance is around 30%), indicating that end-to-end patch-based transformers retain less removable redundancy than object-feature-based models. Thus, LTH observations are architecture-dependent: all tested VLP models exhibit trainable subnetworks, but the maximum non-destructive sparsity differs across backbones.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 benefits from evaluation across three architecturally diverse models (H5), which supports the general claim that LTH holds in VLP. However, the comparison between ViLT and the other models is weakened by the limited task coverage for ViLT (P6, only 2 tasks). P6 creates the risk that ViLT's lower sparsity is task-specific rather than architecture-specific. H5 shows the cross-model evidence but cannot rule out task-specific confounds. The conclusion is credible for the existence of tickets in all three models, but the comparative claim about sparsity differences is less certain due to P6. The prior probability is moderate because the key quantitative comparison (30% vs 70%) rests on a narrow empirical base.

nodes.title: LTH holds across VLP backbones but achievable sparsity differs (LXMERT vs UNITER vs ViLT)

nodes.content: The sparse mask discovered by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) is essential: randomly pruned subnetworks of the same sparsity perform substantially worse than IMP masks across tasks. Furthermore, when the IMP-derived mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}$ is kept but the initialization is changed, performance degrades: (a) reinitializing the mask with pre-trained BERT (a language model) weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ (instead of UNITER pre-trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$) yields lower but still reasonable performance; (b) randomly shuffling UNITER pre-trained weights within layers to produce $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0''$ yields much larger drops, indicating that the specific alignment between the pre-trained weights and the learned mask matters for re-training success.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 is one of the most robust in the paper, supported by controlled experiments (H6) that systematically isolate the contributions of mask and initialization. The baselines are clear and show large performance gaps, and the results are replicated across 7 tasks. There are no load-bearing weak points identified: the comparisons are rigorous and the variance is reported for the key ticket results. The conclusion that both mask and initialization are important is well-supported at the qualitative and quantitative levels. The prior probability is high.

nodes.title: Both the learned mask and the specific pre-trained initialization are important; random pruning and shuffled/alternate initializations degrade performance

nodes.content: In the UNITER finetuning setting evaluated on the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task, resetting the weights to intermediate training checkpoints (rewinding to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i$ for small $i>0$) before re-training pruned subnetworks does not yield notable improvements in downstream accuracy compared to resetting to the original pre-trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$, except for minor gains at extreme sparsities (e.g., 90%).

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 is supported by an experiment only on VQA (P5), and the paper's unsupported claim that other tasks behave similarly. This is a significant load-bearing uncertainty: if rewinding helps on other tasks, the conclusion would be task-specific rather than general. The absence of evidence for other tasks means the derivation is not sufficiently general. No highlight directly addresses this gap; the rewinding curves are shown only for VQA. The conclusion therefore has a low prior probability: it may hold for VQA, but the generalization to "UNITER finetuning" is unjustified. The conclusion should be treated as preliminary and limited to VQA.

nodes.title: Rewinding to early training iterations provides little benefit for UNITER finetuning

nodes.content: Incorporating adversarial training (AT) into the ticket discovery and finetuning pipeline, with adversarial losses $\mathcal{R}_{at}$ (maximizing cross-entropy under an adversarial perturbation $\delta$ bounded by $\epsilon$) and $\mathcal{R}_{kl}$ (KL-divergence based regularization), yields sparse subnetworks that (a) can match or almost match the accuracy of standard (cross-entropy) trained tickets at lower sparsity, and (b) when applied to universal pre-training subnetworks, improves downstream performance: e.g., AT on the universal 60% and 70% sparse subnetworks raises accuracy across multiple tasks relative to standard finetuning, effectively allowing sparse winning tickets that are approximately 10% sparser to reach comparable performance.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 is supported by demonstration on three tasks (Figure 5) and the universal subnetwork improvement (Table 5) (H7). The main weak point is the generalization of the "~10% higher sparsity" claim (P7), which is derived from only three tasks and lacks statistical quantification. H7 shows that AT can enhance tickets and maintain accuracy at higher sparsity, which supports the qualitative direction. However, the specific quantitative figure is not robustly established across tasks. The conclusion that AT can produce/enhance tickets is credible; the claim about a consistent 10% sparsity advantage is less well-supported. AT appears beneficial, but the exact degree of benefit may vary.

nodes.title: Adversarial training can produce or enhance sparse winning tickets and tends to allow ~10% higher sparsity for similar performance

nodes.content: The pairwise overlap ratio between binary masks $\boldsymbol{m}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{m}_j$ (defined as $|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cap\boldsymbol{m}_j|/|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cup\boldsymbol{m}_j|$) varies across source tasks: the pre-training-derived mask shares the highest relative overlap with masks learned from Visual Question Answering (VQA), Natural Language Visual Reasoning for Real (NLVR²), and visual entailment (VE), while masks from GQA, RefCOCO+, and image-text retrieval tasks exhibit lower mutual overlap with others. This heterogeneity in mask overlap correlates with observed transfer behavior among tasks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 8 is based on mask overlap analysis (Figure 8) but lacks a statistical baseline (P8) to determine significance of observed differences. The qualitative observation that masks differ across tasks is visually plausible, but without a null expectation, the strength of this claim is uncertain. The paper does not provide any highlight that directly strengthens this conclusion via rigorous statistical testing. The observed overlaps (e.g., pre-training vs VQA at 0.77) are likely above chance, but for pairs with smaller overlaps (e.g., 0.27), the claim of difference is not quantitatively supported. The conclusion is probable but not rigorously established. The prior is moderate.

nodes.title: Masks learned under different tasks differ; pre-training mask overlaps most with VQA, NLVR², and VE masks

nodes.content:
In the evaluation of UNITER subnetworks on the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task (a seven-way classification from a candidate answer pool given an image and a question), the accuracy used to compute whether a subnetwork reaches 99% of the full model accuracy is measured on an internal "mini-dev" set whose size and composition (e.g., number of examples, image distribution relative to the official VQA test-dev and test-std splits) are not reported.
      Table 1 (Row 4, VQA column)

metadata.failure_mode: If the mini-dev set is not representative of the official VQA test distribution (e.g., it contains disproportionately easy questions or images from a narrow domain), the reported 99% accuracy retention may not hold on the standard VQA test-dev or test-std sets. The concrete failure would be that the claim "relaxed winning tickets exist for VQA at 70% sparsity" is only valid for the mini-dev set, not for the VQA task as normally evaluated, thus narrowing the scope of Conclusion 1 for one of its key supporting tasks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not describe how the mini-dev set was constructed, how many examples it contains, or whether it is representative of the official VQA test distribution. Without this information, the measured accuracy may differ from the accuracy on the standard VQA evaluation protocol. The mini-dev set could be easier (or harder) than the official test set, leading to an overestimate (or underestimate) of the subnetwork's true performance on the VQA task as conventionally benchmarked. The paper's reliance on a non-standard evaluation set for a central claim (that 99% of full accuracy is achieved at 70% sparsity on VQA) introduces uncertainty about the generalizability of that specific quantitative figure.

nodes.title: VQA accuracy measured on unreported mini-dev set

nodes.content:
For the Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) derived ticket performance at the highest sparsity where a relaxed winning ticket is found for each task (subnetwork reinitialized to pre-trained weights and re-trained), the reported accuracies for Visual Question Answering (VQA) at 70% sparsity, GQA at 70%, Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) at 50%, Natural Language Visual Reasoning for Real (NLVR²) at 60%, Stanford Natural Language Inference - Visual Entailment (SNLI-VE) at 60%, Referring Expression Comprehension on RefCOCO+ at 70%, Flickr30k Image Retrieval (IR) at 60%, and Flickr30k Text Retrieval (TR) at 60% are each represented by a single numerical value without error bars, in contrast to the full model results where standard deviations from three runs are provided.
      Table 1 (Rows 2, 4)

metadata.failure_mode: If the single-run ticket performance for, say, VQA at 70% sparsity (69.98) is an optimistic outlier, a repeat with a different seed could yield, e.g., 69.70, which would fall below the 99% threshold (69.93). This would invalidate the conclusion that a relaxed winning ticket exists at 70% sparsity for VQA. More broadly, for any task where the margin above the threshold is small (e.g., NLVR²: 76.32 vs threshold 75.98), a single-run result is insufficient to guarantee the claim robustly.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not report whether the ticket performance is computed from a single random seed or an average across multiple runs, and provides no variance estimate for these key numbers. Given that the full model baseline (Row 2) shows non-zero standard deviations (e.g., 0.06 for VQA, 0.15 for GQA), the ticket performance could plausibly vary across different random seeds. Without multi-seed averaging or error bars, it is uncertain whether the observed performance reliably meets the 99% threshold or could be below it in a different run.

nodes.title: Single-run ticket results for several tasks

nodes.content:
In the Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) procedure applied to UNITER pre-training, each pruning round consists of training for only 10% of the original full pre-training steps, and the total number of pruning rounds is nine before reaching the target sparsity level (e.g., 60% or 70%).
      Table 2; Figure 2 (green curves)

metadata.failure_mode: If the 10% training schedule yields a suboptimal mask, the reported downstream performance of the universal subnetwork (e.g., 98% of full accuracy at 60% sparsity) could be an underestimate (if full pre-training produces a better mask with higher downstream accuracy) or an overestimate (if the reduced training overfits to certain pre-training tasks). This quantitative shift would affect the recommended sparsity levels for universal transfer and weaken the claim that the pre-training mask is the best choice for universal transfer.
metadata.weakness_reason: The decision to use 10% of the original training steps per pruning round is motivated by computational efficiency, but the paper does not validate that the mask identified under this reduced schedule is close to the mask that would be found with full pre-training. The pre-training objectives (Masked Language Modeling, Masked Region Modeling, Image-Text Matching, Word-Region Alignment) may require longer training to fully converge, especially in early pruning rounds where the model is still dense. A mask derived from under-trained weights might not capture the optimal sparse structure for transfer to downstream tasks.

nodes.title: Pre-training IMP uses reduced training steps per round

nodes.content: The pre-training dataset used for mask discovery includes COCO (Common Objects in Context) and Visual Genome, which are also sources of images in several downstream tasks: Visual Question Answering (VQA), GQA, and Referring Expression Comprehension on RefCOCO+ use images from COCO or Visual Genome. The evaluation of the universal transferability of the pre-training mask does not control for this data overlap.

metadata.failure_mode: If the mask's transferability is substantially inflated by data overlap, then the claim that the pre-training ticket "transfers universally" (i.e., to any VL task) would be an overstatement. The conclusion would need to be qualified: the ticket transfers universally among tasks whose image distributions overlap with the pre-training data. The reported average accuracy retention (98% at 60%) would be an overestimate for tasks with completely novel image domains.
metadata.weakness_reason: Because the pre-training data and the downstream task data share images, the good transfer performance of the pre-training mask on VQA, GQA, and RefCOCO+ may partially reflect the mask's familiarity with the specific image distribution, rather than a general ability to preserve cross-modal representations useful for any VL task. The paper does not include any out-of-distribution downstream task (e.g., tasks with entirely disjoint image sets) to isolate the effect of data overlap from true knowledge transfer.

nodes.title: Pre-training data overlaps with downstream task data

nodes.content:
The rewinding experiment, which examines whether resetting the subnetwork weights to an intermediate training checkpoint rather than the pre-trained initialization improves performance after pruning, is conducted only on the Visual Question Answering (VQA) task. The claim that "similar observations are also found on other downstream tasks" is not supported by presented data or citations for those tasks.
      Figure 2(i)

metadata.failure_mode: If rewinding substantially improves performance on tasks other than VQA (e.g., boosting VCR accuracy by 2-3 points at 70% sparsity), then the conclusion that rewinding provides little benefit for UNITER finetuning would be false for those tasks. This would change the practical recommendation: practitioners working on VCR or other tasks might need to employ rewinding to achieve winning tickets, contrary to the paper's uniform claim.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion about rewinding providing little benefit for UNITER finetuning is based on evidence from a single task (VQA). The paper's claim that other tasks exhibit similar behavior is unsupported; no figures or tables are provided for e.g., GQA, VCR, or NLVR². The rewinding effect could be task-dependent: tasks with different optimization landscapes or data sizes (e.g., VCR is more challenging, NLVR² uses image pairs) might benefit more from rewinding, especially at high sparsities.

nodes.title: Rewinding tested only on VQA

nodes.content:
The lottery ticket experiments for ViLT (an end-to-end, patch-based vision-and-language pre-training (VLP) model) are conducted on two downstream tasks: Visual Question Answering (VQA) and Natural Language Visual Reasoning for Real (NLVR²). At 30% sparsity, the subnetwork achieves accuracy values of 70.51 and 75.22 (99.5% and 99.2% of full accuracy, respectively), but no other tasks (e.g., Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR), GQA, RefCOCO+, Flickr30k retrieval) are evaluated for this model.
      Table 4; Figure 7

metadata.failure_mode: If on other tasks (e.g., image-text retrieval or visual entailment) ViLT can achieve relaxed winning tickets at 50-60% sparsity, then the comparative conclusion that ViLT's architecture fundamentally limits its pruneability would be partially incorrect. The difference between ViLT and UNITER/LXMERT would instead reflect task-specific differences, weakening the architectural-dependence claim.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that ViLT's achievable sparsity for relaxed winning tickets is "far lower than LXMERT and UNITER (30% vs. 70%)" rests on performance in only two tasks. ViLT might exhibit higher pruneability on tasks with different characteristics (e.g., retrieval tasks that rely more on language, or tasks with simpler visual reasoning). Without broader task coverage, the observed low sparsity may be a task-specific phenomenon rather than an architectural limitation of ViLT.

nodes.title: ViLT evaluated on only two tasks

nodes.content:
The claim that adversarial training allows "approximately 10% higher sparsity" for comparable performance is derived from experiments on three tasks: Visual Question Answering (VQA), Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR), and RefCOCO+. The comparison shows that, for these tasks, adversarial training at 80% sparsity matches standard training at 70% sparsity, and adversarial training at 70% sparsity matches standard training at 60% sparsity. No explicit error bars or multiple-task averages are provided for this 10% figure.
      Figure 5

metadata.failure_mode: If on other tasks (e.g., NLVR²) the sparsity advantage from adversarial training is only 5% or none, then the claim that AT allows "~10% higher sparsity" would be quantitatively inaccurate for those tasks, leading practitioners to overestimate the compression gain from AT. The qualitative conclusion that AT can produce or enhance tickets would still hold, but the specific quantitative advantage would be overgeneralized.
metadata.weakness_reason: The ~10% sparsity advantage is a qualitative observation from three tasks. The paper does not test other tasks (e.g., NLVR², GQA, image-text retrieval) to see if the advantage generalizes. Moreover, the advantage is expressed as an approximate shift in sparsity, but the paper does not quantify the exact relationship (e.g., regression or statistical test). The benefit might be smaller or larger for other tasks, and the "~10%" figure could be an oversimplification.

nodes.title: AT sparsity advantage quantified on three tasks

nodes.content:
Pairwise Jaccard overlap ratios between binary masks $\boldsymbol{m}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{m}_j$ (defined as $|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cap\boldsymbol{m}_j|/|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cup\boldsymbol{m}_j|$) found by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on different tasks (including pre-training) are reported at 60% and 70% sparsity. These values range from 27% to 77%. No statistical baseline is provided (e.g., expected overlap between two independent random masks at the same sparsity) to determine whether the observed overlaps are significantly different from chance.
      Figure 8

metadata.failure_mode: If some of the reported overlaps are not statistically distinguishable from random masks, then the claim that masks learned under different tasks genuinely differ would be weakened for those task pairs. This would undermine the conclusion's support for the observed transfer behavior, as the correlation between mask overlap and transfer would be confounded by noise.
metadata.weakness_reason: At sparsity levels of 60% and 70% (i.e., 40% and 30% of weights retained), two random masks with independent Bernoulli entries have expected Jaccard overlaps that can be computed analytically. Without such a baseline, it is impossible to assess whether the differences in overlap across task pairs are meaningful or reflect random variation. For example, an overlap of 0.27 (GQA vs RefCOCO+ at 70%) might be near the random expectation, whereas an overlap of 0.77 (pre-training vs VQA at 60%) clearly exceeds it. The paper's qualitative interpretation (masks "differ" and pre-training "shares the most similarity") lacks quantitative support for some of the weaker overlaps.

nodes.title: Mask overlap lacks random baseline

nodes.content: For UNITER (pre-trained transformer with cross-modal attention, taking object-region features and word tokens as input), iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) was applied to seven distinct downstream vision-and-language tasks: VQA (answer selection from a candidate set), GQA (compositional question answering), VCR (visual commonsense reasoning: question-to-answer-and-rationale), NLVR² (natural language reasoning on image pairs), SNLI-VE (visual entailment), RefCOCO+ (referring expression comprehension), and Flickr30k image-text retrieval (both image retrieval and text retrieval, separately). On all seven tasks, the paper reports that a "relaxed winning ticket" (subnetwork reinitialized to pre-trained UNITER weights and re-trained on the task) achieves at least 99% of the full-dense-model accuracy at sparsities of 50-70%, with the specific top sparsity varying by task.

metadata.credit: This multi-task evaluation provides strong support that the existence of relaxed winning tickets in UNITER is not a spurious result of a single task's idiosyncratic objective or dataset. The consistent pattern across tasks that span recognition (RefCOCO+), reasoning (VCR, NLVR², GQA), entailment, and retrieval indicates that the conclusion captures a general property of UNITER's overparameterization for VL tasks. Without this breadth, the claim would be vulnerable to the alternative that only certain tasks (e.g., those with large training sets) admit such tickets. The diversity of tasks underwrites the qualitative direction (tickets exist) and the quantitative range (50-70% sparsity) as a general finding, not a task-specific artifact.

nodes.title: Multi-task consistency of relaxed winning tickets in UNITER

nodes.content: The paper compares the task-specific IMP-winning ticket ($f(x; m_{IMP} \odot \theta_0)$) against three controlled baselines at the same sparsity: (i) random pruning ($f(x; m_{RP} \odot \theta_0)$), where the same number of weights are removed but at random instead of by magnitude; (ii) using pre-trained BERT weights ($\theta_0'$) as initialization with the IMP mask; and (iii) using shuffled UNITER pre-trained weights ($\theta_0''$) with the IMP mask. The results are reported for all seven tasks in Table 1, Rows 5, 6, and 7.

metadata.credit: The random pruning baseline rules out the alternative explanation that any sparse subset of UNITER weights at the same sparsity level would perform equally well; the severe drop (e.g., 69.98 to 60.45 on VQA at 70% sparsity) demonstrates that the IMP mask encodes a non-trivial structure essential for maintaining accuracy. Similarly, the shuffled initialization baseline shows that the mask requires the specific pre-trained weight magnitudes to be effective. These controlled comparisons provide rigorous evidence that both the mask and the initialization are necessary for the winning ticket phenomenon, thus underwriting the mechanism/attribution layer of the conclusion. Without these baselines, the conclusion could be challenged as merely demonstrating that any sparse retraining from pre-trained weights works; the baselines show it does not, giving the "relaxed winning ticket" concept real significance.

nodes.title: Controlled comparative baselines (random pruning, alternative initializations)

nodes.content: A subnetwork discovered by IMP on the UNITER pre-training objectives (using pre-training data with additional pre-training steps) was evaluated on all seven downstream tasks at sparsities of 50%, 60%, 70%, and 80%. The per-task accuracy values are reported in Table 2, along with the overall average accuracy drop relative to the full model (e.g., 1.88% average drop at 60% sparsity, 3.90% at 70% sparsity).

metadata.credit: This systematic evaluation across all tasks and multiple sparsities provides a quantitative characterization of the pre-training ticket's universal transferability. The claim that the ticket transfers is not based on a single task or point estimate but on a matrix of results showing consistent near-full accuracy retention. The inclusion of per-task numbers also allows for honest identification of tasks where transfer is weaker (e.g., VCR at 70% sparsity drops 12.6% relative to full model). This comprehensive measurement underwrites the quantitative magnitude (98%/96% accurate retention) and the scope of generalization, making the conclusion practically useful for compression decisions.

nodes.title: Full-task evaluation of pre-training ticket at multiple sparsities

nodes.content: For six representative target tasks (VQA, VCR, RefCOCO+, NLVR², Flickr30k IR, and Flickr30k TR), the paper plots the transfer performance of ticket masks from eight different source tasks (including pre-training and the other downstream tasks) at sparsities from 10% to 90%. Each subplot in Figure 3 (and Appendix Figure 6 for VE and GQA) shows the accuracy on the target task for each source ticket, allowing cross-task comparison.

metadata.credit: This pairwise transfer matrix provides strong evidence that task-specific masks do not aggressively overfit to their source task, because they retain substantial accuracy when applied to other tasks with different objectives and label spaces. The comprehensive coverage of source-target pairs (6 targets × 8 sources = 48 transfer scenarios) substantially increases the confidence that the observed transferability is a general property of VL task masks, not an artifact of a few similar tasks. This underwrites the qualitative claim that task-specific subnetworks transfer well and gives insight into task relationships (e.g., VQA and GQA masks are mutually beneficial).

nodes.title: Comprehensive pairwise transfer study across tasks

nodes.content: The paper tests the lottery ticket hypothesis on three VLP architectures: UNITER (one-stream transformer with object-region features), LXMERT (two-stream transformer with object-region features), and ViLT (one-stream transformer directly processing image patches and word tokens). For LXMERT, IMP results are reported on three tasks (VQA, GQA, NLVR²); for ViLT, on two tasks (VQA, NLVR²). All three models yield trainable subnetworks that can be pruned to some sparsity, with ViLT having a substantially lower achievable sparsity (~30%) than the other two (~70%).

metadata.credit: This architectural diversity provides evidence that the LTH phenomenon in VLP is not confined to a single model design family. The inclusion of ViLT, which lacks pre-extracted object features, tests whether the existence of winning tickets relies on the object-detection pipeline; the positive result (though at lower sparsity) extends the scope of LTH to end-to-end VLP. The contrast in pruneability between region-feature models and patch-based models yields a nuanced, architecture-dependent conclusion that is more credible than a blanket claim. Without this comparison, the conclusion would be limited to UNITER, and the architectural sensitivity would remain unknown. The multi-architecture evidence underwrites the general-layer claim that LTH holds across VLP backbones, while the sparsity difference supports the specific comparative statement about architectural differences.

nodes.title: Evaluation across three structurally diverse VLP architectures

nodes.content: Using the IMP masks discovered for each UNITER task at their highest effective sparsity, the paper evaluates two alternative initializations: (a) BERT pre-trained weights $\theta_0'$ (which are the language-only initialization that UNITER was subsequently pre-trained from), and (b) shuffled UNITER weights $\theta_0''$ (where weights within each layer are randomly permuted). Results across all tasks (Table 1 Rows 6 and 7) show that $\theta_0'$ yields performance typically between the random pruning and the original ticket (e.g., VQA: 67.98 vs 60.45 and 69.98), while $\theta_0''$ yields severe drops (e.g., VCR: 6.25 vs 53.15).

metadata.credit: These experiments isolate the contribution of the learned mask from that of the specific weight magnitudes. The BERT init experiments show that the mask alone, without the pre-trained UNITER weight magnitudes, loses some but not all of the ticket's advantage—this quantifies the partial importance of the mask structure. The shuffled-weight init experiments show that randomizing weight values within the mask destroys performance, demonstrating that the precise alignment of mask and weight magnitudes is crucial. This controlled isolation provides a rigorous attribution of the winning ticket phenomenon to both components, strengthening the conclusion far beyond what a simple correlation could. Without these experiments, the conclusion would rely on the circumstantial observation that IMP works; with them, it receives mechanistic evidence.

nodes.title: Controlled mask-swapping and weight-shuffling experiments

nodes.content: The paper applies adversarial training (AT) during both the IMP ticket discovery and the subsequent finetuning of subnetworks. For task-specific tickets, Figure 5 shows that AT at 80% sparsity matches or almost matches the accuracy of standard training at 70% sparsity on VQA, VCR, and RefCOCO+. Furthermore, for the universal subnetworks found by pre-training IMP at 60% and 70% sparsities, Table 5 shows that adversarial finetuning improves accuracy on all six evaluated downstream tasks relative to standard finetuning (e.g., VQA: 70.80 vs 70.41 at 60% sparsity; VCR: 51.07 vs 50.37 at 60% sparsity).

metadata.credit: These results show that LTH is not restricted to standard cross-entropy training: adversarial objectives can both find winning tickets and enhance their performance. The improvement on the universal subnetworks (Table 5) is particularly important because it demonstrates that AT can be applied as a practical finetuning technique to boost the accuracy of a compressed model without requiring a separate ticket-discovery round. This extends the regime of validity for LTH to robust training paradigms and provides a concrete avenue for obtaining sparser models with maintained accuracy. Without this evidence, the claim that "LTH also remains relevant when using other training methods" would be unsupported.

nodes.title: Demonstration of LTH under adversarial training with universal subnetwork improvement

steps.reasoning: Define the objects and notation used to state the claim. Let $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ denote the full VLP model (this absorbs both the transformer encoder parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_1}$ and task-specific parameters $\boldsymbol{\phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_2}$). Define a binary pruning mask $\boldsymbol{m}\in\{0,1\}^{d_1}$ that produces a subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$, where $\odot$ is the element-wise product. Define the pre-trained initialization as $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$. Define a "relaxed winning ticket" to be a subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$ which, when reinitialized to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ and re-trained on a downstream task $\mathcal{T}$, reaches at least $99\%$ of the dense full-model accuracy on that task (the paper sets $p=99$ for the relaxed definition).

State the subnetwork discovery procedure used to obtain the masks used in the claim. Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) is used: train the unpruned model to completion on task $\mathcal{T}$, prune a fraction (the authors use 10% per round) of the smallest-magnitude nonzero weights globally, update the mask $\boldsymbol{m}$ accordingly, reset the weights to the chosen rewinding initialization (in this setting typically $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$), and repeat until the desired sparsity is reached; this procedure is summarized in the provided iterative pruning algorithm. This procedure is attributed to Han, Mao, and Dally (2015). 
Han, Mao, and Dally 2015

Describe the concrete experimental protocol used to test existence of relaxed winning tickets in UNITER. For each downstream task $\mathcal{T}$ the authors: (i) run IMP on $\mathcal{T}$ to obtain a task-specific mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{T}}$, producing the subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{T}}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$; (ii) reset the weights to the pre-trained initialization $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$; and (iii) re-train the masked model on the same task $\mathcal{T}$ to measure whether the re-trained subnetwork reaches at least $99\%$ of the full-model accuracy for $\mathcal{T}$. The authors report the IMP curves across sparsities (10% to 90%) as magenta curves in the multi-panel plot summarizing per-task results.
Fig. 2

Present the empirical results that establish the existence of task-specific relaxed winning tickets in UNITER. The authors summarize per-task highest sparsities at which the re-trained IMP subnetworks reach $99\%$ of the dense-model accuracy in a table (Table 1). The reported outcomes (their Row #4) show that for all seven evaluated VL tasks a relaxed winning ticket exists, with the highest achievable sparsities ranging from $50\%$ up to $70\%$ depending on the task: for example, tasks such as VQA and several retrieval/recognition tasks admit relaxed winning tickets at $70\%$ sparsity, whereas the more demanding commonsense reasoning task VCR admits relaxed winning tickets only up to $50\%$ sparsity. These concrete numbers come directly from the presented results in Table 1.
Table 1

Record the authors' interpretation and stated hypothesis about why achievable sparsity differs by task. The authors note that strictly matching the full model is difficult, but the $99\%$ relaxed criterion is achievable in the indicated sparsity ranges; for VCR specifically, the authors hypothesize that commonsense knowledge is harder to learn and that smaller-magnitude weights play a more essential role in commonsense reasoning, making the subnetwork for VCR harder to prune (this hypothesis is stated by the authors without a formal proof).
Table 1

Define the task-agnostic mask and the experimental action that produces it. Let the pre-training-derived IMP mask be denoted $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{P}\in\{0,1\}^{d_1}$; this mask is produced by running Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on the VLP pre-training objective and pre-training data used for UNITER (the pre-training tasks include Masked Language Modeling, Masked Region Modeling, Image-Text Matching, and Word-Region Alignment). The authors explicitly state they perform IMP on the pre-training tasks to obtain a task-agnostic subnetwork candidate.
Chen et al. 2020d

Describe how the task-agnostic subnetwork is evaluated on downstream tasks. The authors form the subnetwork $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{P}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$, reset its weights to the original pre-trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$, and fine-tune this masked model on each downstream VL task in the evaluation suite (the seven tasks: VQA, GQA, VCR, NLVR$^2$, SNLI-VE, RefCOCO+, and Flickr30k retrievals). The performance of these fine-tuned subnetworks is compared to the corresponding full dense-model performance for each task; the data supporting this comparison are reported as green curves (pre-training IMP) in the multi-task plots and are summarized numerically in a results table.
Fig. 2

Present the aggregate quantitative result establishing universal transfer at the claimed sparsities. The authors report the per-task accuracies of the universal pre-training subnetwork at multiple sparsities in a table (Table 2). From those numbers the authors compute average fractions of the full-model accuracy: at $60\%$ sparsity the universal subnetwork matches on average $98\%$ of the full dense-model accuracy across the seven evaluated downstream tasks, and at $70\%$ sparsity it matches on average $96\%$ of the full accuracy. These averages and the per-task numbers are explicitly given in Table 2 and summarized in the text as the universal-transfer result.
Table 2

Record implementation details relevant to how the pre-training IMP was executed, which the authors cite as part of their setup for this result. The authors state that for UNITER pre-training they use the full set of pre-training tasks and datasets (COCO, Visual Genome, Conceptual Captions, SBU Captions), and that during pre-training IMP they run only $10\%$ of the original pre-training training steps in each pruning round and prune for 9 rounds in total (this is reported in the Preliminaries/Methods section). The authors note that this IMP-on-pretraining process thus spends roughly the same compute as pre-training UNITER from scratch.

Note the caveat the authors provide about task exceptions. The authors emphasize that VCR is an outlier that decreases the averaged fraction: if VCR is excluded from the averaging, the universal subnetwork at $60\%/70\%$ sparsities matches $99\%/97\%$ of the full accuracy respectively (this footnoted adjustment is explicitly reported in the paper).
Table 2

State the upstream result used as a starting point: the existence of task-specific relaxed winning tickets in UNITER (conclusion 1) is taken as established and is used as the basis for studying transfer. Symbols carried forward include task-specific IMP masks $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{S}}$ obtained by running IMP on a source task $\mathcal{S}$ and then forming subnetworks $f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{S}}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,\cdot)$ that can be retrained.

Describe the transfer-experiment protocol used by the authors. For a given source task $\mathcal{S}$, the authors obtain a task-specific mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}^{\mathcal{S}}$ by IMP on $\mathcal{S}$; they then reinitialize to $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ and fine-tune that masked model on a different target task $\mathcal{T}$, measuring the downstream performance of the transferred mask across a range of sparsities. The transfer curves (one source per curve) are plotted for each target task to visualize transfer behavior.
Fig. 3

Summarize the empirical observations reported for task-to-task transfer. The authors report three main observations from the transfer plots: (i) subnetworks found by task-specific signals typically perform best on their originating task, particularly in the high-sparsity regime; (ii) subnetworks found on individual downstream tasks nonetheless transfer well to other downstream tasks, indicating that subnetworks encode shared essential representations; and (iii) the subnetwork learned by pre-training typically performs better than most individual downstream-task-derived subnetworks when transferred to other tasks, showing its broad universality. These observations are stated in the paper's transfer-study discussion and are visible in the plotted transfer curves.
Fig. 3

Provide specific examples the authors use to illustrate transfer behavior. The authors point out that for VQA the best external source tickets (excluding VQA itself) are the pre-training ticket and the GQA ticket, attributable to task similarity between VQA and GQA; for image-text retrieval tasks the best source ticket is often the pre-training ticket because pre-training includes an image-text matching objective similar to retrieval. These specific cross-task source-target relationships are reported in the text accompanying the transfer figures.
Fig. 3

State the general conclusion about task-specific subnetwork transferability that the authors derive from these results. Based on the transfer curves and the per-task analyses, the authors conclude that subnetworks obtained by IMP on a specific downstream source task $\mathcal{S}$ typically maintain strong performance when re-trained on other target tasks $\mathcal{T}$: across evaluated task pairs, task-specific tickets generally transfer reasonably, often retaining the majority of the source-ticket's effectiveness on different target tasks across a variety of pruning sparsities.

Define the model families and their input modalities to clarify architecture differences. UNITER is a one-stream model that consumes object-region image features and word embeddings; LXMERT is a two-stream model that also uses object-region inputs but separates visual and textual streams before cross-modality interaction; ViLT is an end-to-end one-stream, patch-based model that directly consumes image patches and word tokens and relies on a single unified transformer to model intra- and inter-modality interactions. These architectural descriptions are provided in the Preliminaries.

Describe the experiments run to test LTH across backbones. The authors run the same IMP-based pruning and retraining procedure on LXMERT and ViLT (in addition to the main UNITER experiments) and report per-task ticket curves and per-sparsity summary tables for these models (plots for LXMERT appear in Figure 4 and numbers in Table 3; plots for ViLT appear in Figure 7 and numbers in Table 4).
Fig. 4
Fig. 7

Report the results for LXMERT that support the claim that LTH holds similarly to UNITER. For LXMERT the authors present Table 3 showing that IMP can identify relaxed winning tickets at sparsities comparable to UNITER (the table shows that at $70\%$ sparsity LXMERT subnetworks achieve accuracies very close to the full-model references and meet the relaxed $99\%$ criterion reported in the table rows for "Lottery Tickets"). These numerical results indicate that LTH observations are present for LXMERT with achievable sparsities comparable to UNITER.
Table 3

Report the results for ViLT that support the claim that achievable sparsity differs by architecture. For ViLT the authors present Table 4 and additional plots (Figure 7) showing that the highest sparsity the authors can achieve without impairing performance is substantially lower (around $30\%$; the paper additionally notes at other places that ViLT's effective highest sparsity is only around $30\%$--$40\%$). Table 4 reports accuracies for ViLT at $30\%$ sparsity and compares them to random pruning and $99\%$ references; these results show that ViLT cannot be pruned to the same degree as UNITER/LXMERT without performance loss.
Table 4
Fig. 7

Explain the authors' stated reason for the architecture-dependent pruning frontier. The authors attribute ViLT's lower achievable sparsity to its end-to-end, patch-based design: because ViLT uses a single unified transformer to absorb all modeling of visual and textual interactions (and directly processes image patches rather than fixed object-region features), there is less removable redundancy in the transformer parameters compared to models (UNITER/LXMERT) that rely on pre-extracted object features; this explanation is stated as the authors' interpretation in the paper.

Conclude the architecture-dependent nature of LTH in VLP as stated. Combining the LXMERT and ViLT results with the UNITER findings, the authors summarize that LTH holds across different VLP backbones (i.e., trainable subnetworks exist in all tested models) but the maximum non-destructive sparsity differs across architectures, with ViLT having a substantially lower pruning frontier than UNITER and LXMERT.

Start from the established existence of task-specific relaxed tickets (conclusion 1) and describe the controlled comparisons the authors perform to test the importance of the learned mask and the initialization. Define the following: $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{IMP}}$ denotes the IMP-derived mask for a task; $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{RP}}$ denotes a randomly generated pruning mask with the same sparsity (random pruning); $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ denotes the UNITER pre-trained weights; $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ denotes pre-trained BERT weights used as an alternate initialization; and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0''$ denotes UNITER pre-trained weights randomly shuffled within each layer to destroy alignment.

Describe the experiments and where the comparative results are reported. The authors compare (i) training the IMP-discovered masked network from $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ (the IMP baseline), (ii) training a randomly pruned model with mask $\boldsymbol{m}_{\text{RP}}$ from $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ (random pruning baseline), (iii) training the IMP mask but initialized with $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ (pre-trained BERT initialization), and (iv) training the IMP mask but initialized with $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0''$ (shuffled UNITER weights). These comparisons and their numeric results are presented in Table 1 (Rows #4, #5, #6, and #7) and are also visualized across sparsities in the plotted curves.
Table 1
Fig. 2

Report the quantitative evidence that the learned mask matters: random pruning performs substantially worse than IMP masks. From Table 1, Row #4 (the IMP model at the reported highest relaxed sparsities) the VQA result is $69.98\pm0.05$, whereas Row #5 (random pruning at the same sparsity) reports VQA $60.45$: this large gap illustrates that a randomly pruned subnetwork of the same sparsity performs far worse than the IMP-discovered mask on VQA. Similar performance gaps are visible across other tasks in Table 1, establishing that the specific sparse structure found by IMP is crucial to obtain high accuracy.
Table 1

Report the empirical evidence that the specific pre-trained initialization matters. From Table 1, keeping the IMP-derived mask but initializing with pre-trained BERT weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ (Row #6) yields, for example on VQA, $67.98$ versus $69.98\pm0.05$ when initialized with UNITER $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$; this indicates a moderate drop but still reasonable performance. In contrast, initializing the IMP mask with the shuffled UNITER weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0''$ (Row #7) yields a much larger drop (VQA $60.46$), comparable to random pruning in some tasks. These quantitative comparisons in Table 1 support the authors' claim that both the learned mask and the specific alignment of the pre-trained initialization are important for retraining success.
Table 1

Record the authors' qualitative interpretation of the initialization results. The authors hypothesize that the relatively good performance when using pre-trained BERT weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ is partially because $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0'$ was used as the initialization for pre-training UNITER, so UNITER's weight structure may inherit patterns from BERT; by contrast, shuffling $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ to form $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0''$ destroys alignment between weights and mask and causes much larger performance drops. This interpretation is stated by the authors as an explanatory hypothesis.

State the rewinding concept used in the paper and define notation. Rewinding means resetting weights to an intermediate training checkpoint $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i$ (the weights after $i$ steps of training) rather than to the original pre-trained initialization $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ before retraining the masked subnetwork. The authors reference prior work that found rewinding useful for identifying winning tickets in large networks.
Renda, Frankle, and Carbin 2020

Describe the experimental test the authors perform to evaluate rewinding in the UNITER finetuning context. The authors run IMP to obtain masks, and then in representative experiments on VQA they reset weights to various rewinding points $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i$ before retraining the masked model; they compare downstream accuracy across rewinding choices and across sparsities. The VQA rewinding results are plotted as a separate sub-figure in the multipanel figure (Figure 2(i)).
Fig. 2(i)

Report the empirical finding about effectiveness of rewinding in this setting. The authors observe that rewinding to early intermediate checkpoints $\boldsymbol{\theta}_i$ (for small $i>0$) does not produce notable improvements in downstream accuracy relative to resetting to pre-trained $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ in the UNITER finetuning experiments on VQA; only minor gains are observed at extreme sparsities (for example the authors note a minor improvement at $90\%$ sparsity). These observations are reported directly in the VQA rewinding plot and in the accompanying text.
Fig. 2(i)

State the authors' conclusion for UNITER finetuning based on these experiments. The authors conclude that, in their UNITER finetuning setting, rewinding to early training iterations provides little benefit for recovering downstream accuracy of pruned subnetworks, except possibly for small improvements only at extreme sparsities.

State upstream results used as starting points. Use (a) existence of relaxed tickets in UNITER (conclusion 1) and (b) the transferability of pre-training-derived universal subnetwork (conclusion 2) as established facts to motivate studying adversarial training (AT) combined with IMP.

Reproduce the adversarial training objective and the specific loss components the paper uses (these equations are verbatim from the paper and define the training procedure used to find and refine tickets under adversarial training). Define symbols: $\mathcal{L}_{std}(\cdot)$ is the cross-entropy loss on clean data; $\mathcal{R}_{at}(\cdot)$ is the label-preserving adversarial training loss; $\mathcal{R}_{kl}(\cdot)$ is an adversarial regularization term; $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ denotes adversarial perturbations constrained by $\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|\le\epsilon$; $L(\cdot)$ denotes cross-entropy; $L_{kl}(p,q)=\mathrm{KL}(p||q)+\mathrm{KL}(q||p)$.
The outer minimization objective is:
$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi}\mathbb{E}_{(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{std}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi)+\mathcal{R}_{at}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi)+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{R}_{kl}(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi)\right].
$$
The adversarial loss components are defined as:
$$
\mathcal{R}_{at}(\cdot)=\max_{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|\le\epsilon} L(f(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi),\boldsymbol{y}),
$$
$$
\mathcal{R}_{kl}(\cdot)=\max_{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|\le\epsilon} L_{kl}(f(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi),f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi)).
$$
For the inner maximization (solving for adversarial $\boldsymbol{\delta}$) the authors use Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), which they present via the iterative update:
$$
\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}\|\le\epsilon}\left(\boldsymbol{\delta}_t+\alpha\frac{g(\boldsymbol{\delta}_t)}{\|g(\boldsymbol{\delta}_t)\|_F}\right),
$$
where $g(\boldsymbol{\delta}_t)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}L(f(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta};\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta},\phi),\boldsymbol{y})$. The PGD approach is credited to Madry et al. 2017.
Madry et al. 2017

Describe the experimental comparison and where the evidence appears. The authors compare standard (cross-entropy) finetuning of masked models versus adversarial training (AT) finetuning of masked models across multiple sparsities and multiple tasks. They present plots of adversarial-ticket performance per task (Figure 5) and a numerical summary for the universal pre-training subnetworks at $60\%$ and $70\%$ sparsities under standard vs adversarial finetuning in Table 5.
Fig. 5
Table 5

Report the empirical results showing that adversarial training can improve or allow sparser tickets. From Table 5 the authors report for the universal pre-training subnetworks: at $60\%$ sparsity, standard finetuning yields VQA $70.41$, while adversarial finetuning yields VQA $70.80$ (an improvement); similarly for other tasks listed in Table 5 the adversarially finetuned masked models obtain equal or slightly higher accuracies than standard finetuning at the same sparsity. Additionally, the authors note (and plot in Figure 5) that a ticket trained with AT at $80\%$ (or $70\%$) sparsity can match or nearly match the accuracy of a standard-trained ticket at $70\%$ (or $60\%$) sparsity respectively — i.e., adversarial training effectively permits approximately a $10\%$ sparser mask to reach comparable performance to standard training. These numeric comparisons and the stated approximate 10% sparsity gap are made explicitly by the authors in the main text and in the Table/Figure captions.
Table 5
Fig. 5

State the authors' conclusion combining these observations. The authors conclude that adversarial training can be used to produce or enhance sparse winning tickets: AT either produces tickets that match or nearly match the accuracy of standard-trained tickets at the same sparsity, or permits sparser tickets (roughly $\sim10\%$ sparser) to achieve comparable performance; moreover, applying AT to the universal pre-training subnetworks improves downstream accuracy across multiple tasks, demonstrating AT's utility in enhancing sparse-ticket performance in the VL setting.

Start from established masks and define the overlap metric the authors use. For two binary masks $\boldsymbol{m}_i,\boldsymbol{m}_j\in\{0,1\}^{d_1}$ the pairwise overlap ratio is defined as
$$
\frac{|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cap\boldsymbol{m}_j|}{|\boldsymbol{m}_i\cup\boldsymbol{m}_j|},
$$
where $|\cdot|$ denotes the count of nonzero entries. This formula is explicitly given in the paper when discussing mask similarity.

Describe how the authors compute and present the mask-overlap results. The authors compute the relative overlap ratios between masks learned by IMP under different training signals (each downstream task and pre-training), at selected sparsities (e.g., $60\%$ and $70\%$), and present the pairwise overlaps in a heatmap figure (Figure 8). The figure cells report the relative overlap percentages between each pair of task-derived masks.
Fig. 8

Report the empirical pattern the authors extract from the overlap matrix. From the overlap analysis (Figure 8) the authors find that masks learned under different tasks differ substantially (i.e., overlaps vary by task pair). Concretely, the pre-training-derived mask shares the highest relative overlap with masks learned from VQA, NLVR$^2$, and Visual Entailment (VE). In contrast, masks derived from GQA, RefCOCO+, and image-text retrieval tasks show relatively low overlap with masks from other tasks. These qualitative statements are explicitly written in the paper's text describing the overlap figure.
Fig. 8

State the authors' connection between heterogeneity of masks and transfer behavior. The authors note that the heterogeneity in mask overlap correlates with observed transfer behavior: tasks whose masks overlap more (for example pre-training with VQA/NLVR$^2$/VE) tend to exhibit better mutual transfer in the transfer plots, whereas tasks with lower mask overlap exhibit weaker transfer relationships. This correlation between mask similarity and transfer patterns is asserted by the authors based on the juxtaposition of the overlap heatmap and the transfer results.

open_questions.content: The study identifies several acknowledged limitations and unresolved scientific issues for future work. First, efficiency and practical speedup: while IMP discovers sparse subnetworks, the work did not measure real-world inference speedups on hardware and runtimes that support unstructured pruning; evaluating end-to-end latency and utilizing pruning-friendly runtimes (e.g., XNNPACK or similar) is left unresolved. Second, object-detection and end-to-end VLP pruning: for region-feature-based models (UNITER, LXMERT) the object detector was kept intact, so whether and how matching subnetworks exist within object detection components and in full end-to-end detection+fusion pipelines remains open. Third, strict winning tickets (exact matching of full-model accuracy) were generally not found for many VL tasks; only "relaxed" (99%) tickets were observed at substantial sparsity, and understanding whether strict matching is achievable and under what conditions is unresolved. Fourth, task-specific differences in pruneability (e.g., VCR being harder to prune without loss and ViLT admitting much lower maximum sparsity) are empirically observed but not fully explained mechanistically; determining the causes (e.g., task complexity, reliance on small-weight contributions, architectural concentration of capacity) is left for future investigation. Finally, the computational cost of IMP for very large pre-training regimes motivates exploring more efficient ticket-finding methods (e.g., one-shot pruning heuristics or gradient-flow preserving initializations) that were not resolved here.
